mcqs.question: Calling fread() in C sometimes does not trigger a read() syscall at all. Why?
options: fread() is not a real function, it's a macro that always resolves at compile time
The kernel caches the result of the first fread() call for the process's lifetime
fread() always bypasses the kernel entirely regardless of buffer state
fread() can serve data from a userspace buffer glibc already filled, only syscalling when that buffer is empty
mcqs.explanation: Standard I/O buffers data in user space; fread() only issues a real read() syscall when its buffer is exhausted, which is why library calls and syscalls aren't a 1:1 mapping. It isn't a compile-time macro, there's no such kernel-side per-process cache, and it does sometimes syscall.

mcqs.question: getpid() and uname() belong to which syscall category?
options: Device management
Information maintenance — they query state without changing anything
Communication
Process control
mcqs.explanation: Both calls report existing state (a process ID, kernel/OS identity) without altering it, which is exactly the information-maintenance category. They don't configure hardware, move data between processes, or control process lifecycle.

mcqs.question: Why is the Linux syscall table append-only, with numbers never reused or reordered?
options: Because syscall numbers form part of the binary ABI — a shifted number would break already-compiled binaries
Because the kernel enforces alphabetical ordering of syscall names
Because reordering would violate a licensing requirement
Because syscall numbers must match ASCII codes of their first letter
mcqs.explanation: Compiled binaries hard-code the syscall number they expect a given operation to use; changing that mapping later would silently break every existing binary. There's no alphabetical, licensing, or ASCII-code constraint involved.

mcqs.question: In the strace output for `cat hello.txt`, a `read()` call returns 0. What does that indicate?
options: A permissions error occurred while reading
The read timed out waiting for data
End of file — there is no more data left to read from that descriptor
The file descriptor was invalid
mcqs.explanation: A read() return value of 0 is the standard EOF signal, distinct from a negative return value which would indicate an error (and errors show a specific errno, not silently 0). It's not a timeout or an invalid-descriptor signal — those produce -1 with a corresponding errno.

mcqs.question: What's the fundamental difference between a system call and a signal?
options: Signals are only used for terminating processes, while syscalls do everything else
A syscall is synchronous and initiated by the process; a signal is asynchronous and delivered to the process by the kernel
There is no real difference — they're two names for the same mechanism
Syscalls can only be sent between processes, never to the kernel
mcqs.explanation: A syscall is a process actively asking the kernel for something and blocking for the response; a signal is the kernel interrupting a process asynchronously, at a time the process didn't choose. Signals do more than terminate (many are caught and handled), and syscalls target the kernel, not other processes directly.

mcqs.question: Why does Linux's vDSO let clock_gettime() avoid a full mode switch?
options: It caches the very first timestamp forever and returns that same value
It disables interrupts so the read appears instantaneous
It maps kernel-updated time data into the process's own address space, readable entirely in user mode
It runs the call on a separate dedicated CPU core
mcqs.explanation: vDSO maps a page of kernel-maintained data directly into user space, so reading the time is a plain memory read with no trap needed — dramatically cheaper than a real syscall. It doesn't cache a single stale value, disable interrupts, or require a dedicated core.
